summary: Sirach 20 gathers sayings about timing, speech, shame, gifts, lies, and wisdom that is either displayed well or wasted. The chapter begins with reproof and silence, moves through reversals of gain and loss, warns about foolish giving and loose speech, and ends by saying hidden wisdom is as unprofitable as hidden treasure.
whyItMatters: This chapter sits in Sirach's larger training in ordinary conduct. It shows wisdom not only as having right ideas, but as knowing when to speak, how to give, and how to avoid speech that damages oneself and others.

context.author: Yeshua (Jesus) son of Eleazar son of Sira, a Jerusalem teacher and scribe; his unnamed grandson later translated the book into Greek.
context.audience: Students seeking disciplined wisdom in Jerusalem, and later Greek-reading Jews in Egypt or the wider diaspora.
context.date: The Hebrew work was composed in the early second century BC, likely around 180-175 BC; the Greek translation followed after the grandson came to Egypt, commonly understood as 132 BC.
context.setting: Jerusalem under Hellenistic rule, with temple worship, scribal learning, and Jewish life inside a Greek-speaking Mediterranean world.
context.literaryForm: Wisdom instruction in compact sayings and vivid comparisons, meant to form judgment in speech, friendship, money, status, and public conduct.

outline.heading: Reproof and timely silence
outline.note: The chapter opens by weighing correction, anger, silence, talkativeness, and the danger of seizing authority for oneself.

outline.heading: Gain, loss, and gifts
outline.note: A series of reversals shows that prosperity may come through misfortune, gifts may harm rather than help, and a fool's giving can turn friendship into resentment.

outline.heading: Slips of the tongue
outline.note: Speech is compared to stumbling, an ill-timed tale, and a parable badly delivered by a fool.

outline.heading: Bashfulness and lies
outline.note: The sayings move from lack that restrains sin, to destructive bashfulness, to lying as a lasting dishonor.

outline.heading: Wisdom, influence, and hidden profit
outline.note: The chapter closes with prudent speech, work, the corrupting effect of favors and gifts, and the uselessness of wisdom kept out of sight.

keyVerses.text: There is a reproof that is not timely; and there is a person who is wise enough to keep silent.
keyVerses.why: This verse names the chapter's central concern: wisdom depends on timing, not merely on having something true to say.

keyVerses.text: A wise man will be silent until his time has come, but the braggart and fool will miss his time.
keyVerses.why: The contrast between the wise person and the fool shows how speech can fail by being premature, boastful, or badly timed.

keyVerses.text: A slip on a pavement is better than a slip with the tongue. So the fall of the wicked will come speedily.
keyVerses.why: This vivid comparison anchors the chapter's warning that careless speech can be more damaging than a physical stumble.

keyVerses.text: Wisdom that is hidden, and treasure that is out of sight— what profit is in either of them?
keyVerses.why: The ending balances the earlier praise of silence: wisdom must not be noisy, but it also must not be uselessly concealed.

questions.question: Why does the chapter praise silence so much?
questions.answer: The chapter does not treat all silence as wise. It distinguishes the person who keeps silent because he has no answer from the person who keeps silent because he knows when to speak. Wisdom here means judgment about timing, not permanent withdrawal from speech.

questions.question: What is a "reproof" in this chapter?
questions.answer: A reproof is a corrective word or rebuke. The chapter says correction can be good, but it can also be mistimed. The point is not that correction should never happen, but that anger and bad timing can make it harmful.

questions.question: Why is verse 4 such a harsh comparison?
questions.answer: Verse 4 compares violent judgment to a eunuch’s desire to deflower a virgin. The sexual image is jarring, and the verse does not explain the comparison in detail. In context, it criticizes judgment carried out with violence as a distorted use of authority.

questions.question: What does the chapter mean by gain turning into loss?
questions.answer: Verses 9-12 collect reversals: misfortune can lead to prosperity, gifts may fail to profit, and a cheap purchase may become costly. These sayings warn first-time readers not to judge an outcome too quickly by its opening appearance.

questions.question: Why can a gift be bad?
questions.answer: The chapter describes a fool whose gift is not generous because he expects repeated repayment, gives little, insults much, and quickly asks back what he lent. The problem is not gift-giving itself, but giving that manipulates, humiliates, or creates resentment.

questions.question: Is the chapter saying poverty can be morally useful?
questions.answer: Verse 21 says one person is hindered from sinning through lack, meaning lack of means can prevent a wrong action from being carried out. It does not say poverty is good in itself or that poor people are more virtuous. The saying is about restraint by circumstance, not a complete theology of poverty.

questions.question: What is "bashfulness" doing here?
questions.answer: In verses 22-23, bashfulness names a shame or embarrassment that leads someone to self-destruction or to making promises he should not make. The chapter treats this as a failure of wise judgment. It is not condemning ordinary shyness, but warning against social pressure that makes a person act falsely.

questions.question: Why does Sirach say a thief is better than a continual liar?
questions.answer: Verse 25 is a sharp comparison, not a full ranking of every possible wrongdoing. It stresses that continual lying destroys trust and leads to destruction. The next verse explains the liar's destination as dishonor and continual shame.

questions.question: Does the ending contradict the earlier praise of silence?
questions.answer: No. Earlier verses praise silence that waits for the right time, while verses 30-31 criticize wisdom kept hidden so completely that it profits no one. The chapter holds both together: careless speech is dangerous, but useful wisdom must eventually become visible.

glossary.def: A corrective word or rebuke. In this chapter, reproof must be timely and can be turned aside when favors and gifts silence correction.
A boastful person who speaks at the wrong time. The chapter pairs the braggart with the fool as someone who misses the proper moment.
A shame or embarrassment that can lead someone to self-destruction or false promises. The chapter treats it as dangerous when it overrides wise judgment.
A compact saying or comparison used to teach. Verse 20 says a parable from a fool's mouth fails because it is not spoken at the proper time.
Wrongdoing or guilt. In verse 28, pleasing great men is described as a way someone may get pardon for iniquity.
